captions.instagram:
What keeps things moving in circles?

Whirl a ball on a string, then cut it: the ball flies off straight, not outwards. Spin-dry clothes at 400 g, feel 10,000 g at a mixer's blade tip, take a bend on a wet road, loop the loop, ride India's wall of death, and bust the myths of centrifugal force and the backwards-draining sink.

→ Going round needs a pull to the centre: F = m v² ÷ r. Double the speed, four times the pull.
→ Cut the string and the ball flies straight on along the tangent, not outwards.
→ A washer drum at 1,200 rpm pushes clothes in 400 times harder than gravity. The water flies straight out.
→ A blood centrifuge at 1,000 g packs red cells down and leaves yellow plasma on top in minutes.
→ On a flat bend only tyre grip turns the car. Too fast for √(μ g r) and it slides off the outside.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/circularclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: What keeps things moving in circles? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Whirl a ball on a string, then cut it: the ball flies off straight, not outwards. Spin-dry clothes at 400 g, feel 10,000 g at a mixer's blade tip, take a bend on a wet road, loop the loop, ride India's wall of death, and bust the myths of centrifugal force and the backwards-draining sink.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/circularclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/circularclear

In this video:
• Turning needs a pull. Going round a circle means your direction changes all the time, so you are accelerating towards the centre: a = v² ÷ r.
• Spinning machines. Every point on a spinning part moves at v = ω r and needs ω² r.
• On the road. On a flat bend only tyre friction turns you, so the top speed is √(μ g r) whatever the mass: 71 km/h on a dry 50 m bend.
• Rides and space. A loop needs v ≥ √(g r) at the top, so the cart must enter at √(5 g r).
• Myths and limits. Nothing flings you outwards: centrifugal force is inertia seen from a turning frame.
